query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy, introducing a minor (~5 at%) aluminum addition will promote the in situ formation of coherent, nanometer-scale, Ni3Ti-type (γ′) precipitates within the matrix, thereby enhancing the alloy’s elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance (by roughly 20%) relative to the same alloy without the aluminum addition.
generation.material_initial_state: A Ti-Ni–primary high-entropy alloy designed with roughly equal high loadings of titanium and nickel (e.g. ~35 at% Ti, ~35 at% Ni) with the balance provided by other elements (such as Co, Fe or Cr) to satisfy the ≥5-elements, 5–35 at% definition, and initially exhibiting a single-phase solid solution (e.g., FCC) with moderate high-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.intervention: Add approximately 5 atomic percent aluminum to the base high-entropy alloy composition.
generation.conditions: The alloy should be processed under conditions (such as rapid solidification by directed energy deposition) that yield a fine microstructure and minimal grain coarsening, and then tested at elevated temperatures in the range of approximately 800–1000 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The aluminum addition is expected to induce the controlled precipitation of coherent, fine Ni3Ti-type (γ′) ordered nanoprecipitates within the predominantly disordered matrix.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum, having a comparatively small atomic radius and a strong chemical affinity with both Ti and Ni, encourages local chemical ordering. This leads to the nucleation and growth of coherent γ′ precipitates which act as obstacles to dislocation motion (through formation of anti-phase boundaries), thereby increasing yield strength and improving resistance to high-temperature creep.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified alloy, the Al–modified alloy will display an enhanced yield strength (approximately a 20% increase) and improved creep resistance when operated in the 800–1000 °C range.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the titanium- and nickel-primary HEA without aluminum addition, exhibiting only a single-phase solid solution and moderate elevated-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to hold for high-entropy alloy compositions where each element constitutes between 5–35 at% and where processing (e.g., rapid cooling via DED) successfully limits grain coarsening. Excessive aluminum (>~7 at%) might lead to overabundant or brittle intermetallic phases, while too little (<~3 at%) may be insufficient to nucleate the desired precipitates.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence from Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti systems (e.g., PMC11396108::web::002::1_introduction) and precipitation-hardened medium-entropy alloys (PMC10532893::web::019::5_conclusions) supports the role of Al in promoting a strengthening ordered phase, its exact behavior when titanium and nickel are primary constituents is uncertain. The optimal aluminum level and precipitate stability in this new compositional regime remain to be fully characterized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Ti-Ni–primary high-entropy alloys with identical processing: one set with the base composition and the other with an additional ~5 at% Al. Use a rapid solidification method (e.g., directed energy deposition) to obtain similar microstructures in both sets. Perform high-temperature tensile tests and creep experiments at 800–1000 °C. Additionally, use X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy to assess the presence, morphology, and distribution of any γ′ precipitates.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (TEM/SEM) to detect coherent γ′ precipitates
Phase identification (XRD) to confirm ordered precipitate formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminum-modified alloy does not exhibit a significant improvement (e.g., <5% increase) in yield strength or creep resistance relative to the baseline alloy, or if microstructural characterization does not reveal the presence of a fine dispersion of coherent γ′ precipitates, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The addition of elements with similar metallic atomic radii but different crystallographic structures (Al and Ti) to the Co-Ni-Fe alloy caused higher solution strengthening by the element with a different crystallographic structure than the solvent. The solid solution strengthening coming from addition of 5 at. pct Al to the Co-Ni-Fe alloy is negligible, while the addition of 5 at. pct of Ti significantly increases the solid solution strengthening. The precipitation hardening effect related to the presence of (CoNi)3Ti phase caused by the addition of 5 at. pct Ti is comparable with the total effect of the 5 at. pct Al and 5 at. pct Ti addition, which caused the precipitation of γ′ ((NiCo)3AlTi). Precipitation hardening is much greater in the investigated alloys than the solid solution hardening. We showed a successful way for effectively strengthening the FCC-HEA system (NiCoFe) using a small Ti addition. The microstructure obtained in the M3 alloy consists of precipitates with an L12 structure and structurally coherent with FCC matrix. We showed one of the ways of searching for new high-entropy alloys.

In particular, the extraordinary ductility and fracture toughness of FCC-structured HEAs at ambient temperature and cryogenic temperatures have garnered significant attention [,,,,]. The low yield strength of FCC-structured HEAs, which is typically just 200 MPa in the as-cast form, is a significant disadvantage, as it is significantly less than the necessary strength of metallic structural materials [,]. To overcome these limitations in mechanical properties, a proposed method is to manufacture an HEA composed of a multicomponent FCC-HEA matrix with an ordered FCC structure (L12) precipitated phase, i.e., the γ′ phase, by adding Al + Ti. An HEA based on a γ + γ′ alloy system exhibited excellent thermal stability, coarsening resistance, and strength retention around a temperature of 800 °C [,,,]. The γ′ phase is an ordered phase with an almost exact stoichiometric composition ((Ni, Co)3(Ti, Al)) in the Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA, with γ′ depending on the Al + Ti content []. Numerous studies have been conducted on the γ′ phase’s formation and mechanical properties [,]. A high content of Al + Ti leads to the formation of precipitate phases such as Ni2AlTi.
